en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
Chattupāhanavagga 94.
The Training Rule on Not Taking Leave At that time the Buddha,
the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, nuns were sitting on seats in front of a monk without having asked permission.
The monks were indignant, complained, and grumbled, saying, "How can these nuns sit on seats in front of a monk without asking permission? ... [as before] ...
“Is it true, monks, that nuns sit on a seat in front of a monk without having asked permission?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them … [as before] …
“How indeed, monks, can nuns sit down on a seat in front of a monk without having asked permission? This, monks,
does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence … And so,
monks, let the nuns recite this training rule:”
“Whatever nun, however, should sit on a seat in front of a monk without having asked permission, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
“Whatever nun” means whichever nun of such a kind... [and so forth].
"A bhikkhunī" ...
[as before] ... this is the kind of bhikkhunī intended in this context.
"In front of a bhikkhu":
In front of one who is fully ordained.
"Without having asked" means without having obtained permission.
"Should sit on a seat":
even if one sits on the bare ground, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one sits on a seat without having asked permission, and one perceives that one has not asked permission, it is an offense of expiation.
If she sits on a seat without having asked permission, and she is in doubt, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

If she sits on a seat without having asked permission, but perceives that she has asked permission, there is an offense of expiation. If she sits on a seat after having asked permission, but perceives that she has not asked permission, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she has asked for permission but is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If she has asked for permission and perceives that she has asked for permission, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
He sits on a seat after having asked for permission,
except in the case of illness or in times of emergency.
"Of one who is insane,
of one who is a first-offender.
The eleventh training rule is concluded.
